lessons.title: Modeling Slippage: Fixed, Percentage, and Volume-Based Approaches

children.text: Lessons 1 and 2 built the two pieces, spread cost and market impact. In practice, backtests rarely implement the full machinery for every single trade, especially early in a project. Three levels of sophistication show up again and again in real codebases, and choosing the wrong one for your strategy is a quiet way to reintroduce the exact gap this course exists to close.

Subtract a flat rupee amount from every trade, say ₹50 per round trip, no matter what is traded or how much. This is the crudest model available. Its one virtue is that it takes thirty seconds to implement and is better than assuming zero slippage. Its flaw is that it does not scale with trade value at all, so it is simultaneously too large for a tiny order and absurdly too small for a large one.

Apply a flat percentage of trade value, for example 0.10% round trip, to every trade regardless of stock. This is a real improvement, since cost now at least scales with trade size. It is still blind to liquidity: a ₹5 lakh order in a Nifty 50 name and a ₹5 lakh order in a thinly traded smallcap are charged identically, even though Lessons 1 and 2 already showed those two trades face very different spreads and very different market impact.

Combine the two lessons that came before this one: a liquidity-tier spread cost, plus a square-root market impact term driven by order value relative to average daily traded value. This is the most realistic of the three, and the only one that correctly distinguishes a small liquid trade from a large illiquid one. It is also the most demanding, since it needs ADV data per stock, per day, not just price data.

cells: Rough sanity checks only, never for real decisions
Any strategy trading beyond a handful of Nifty 50 names, or at meaningful size

body.title: Estimated Slippage Cost Across Three Models

body.text: Fixed slippage is off by nearly 2000 times on Scenario C, ₹50 estimated against a volume-based estimate of ₹95,235. Percentage-based is closer but still off by roughly 19 times on that same scenario, because it has no way to know the order is 33% of the stock's daily volume. Both simpler models happen to look reasonable on Scenario A, small order, liquid name, which is exactly the trap: they get validated on easy cases and then quietly fail on the trades that matter most.

children.text: Choosing a Model for Your Backtest

Use fixed slippage only for a first sanity pass, never as the basis for a real go or no-go decision. Percentage-based is a defensible shortcut if, and only if, a strategy trades exclusively liquid, large-cap names at modest size relative to ADV, roughly the conditions of Scenario A. The moment a strategy touches midcaps, smallcaps, or order sizes that are a meaningful share of daily volume, which describes most strategies interesting enough to be worth building, volume-based slippage stops being optional.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: A strategy trades exclusively Nifty 50 stocks, always at a small fraction of ADV. It is about to expand into Nifty Smallcap 250 names at sizes near 20% of ADV. What is the most defensible next step for its cost model?
options: No change needed, percentage-based slippage worked fine before
Switch to fixed slippage, since it is simpler to maintain
Move to a volume-based model before going live in the new universe, since liquidity and participation rate now vary far more across trades
Ignore slippage for the new universe since it only affects a small part of the portfolio
body.explanation: The conditions that made percentage-based slippage defensible, liquid names, modest participation rates, no longer hold once the strategy trades smallcaps at 20% of ADV. This lesson's comparison table showed volume-based estimates diverging from percentage-based ones by an order of magnitude in exactly this kind of scenario.

body.text: Fixed and percentage-based slippage models are not wrong so much as they are untested, they happen to look fine on small, liquid trades and fail quietly on exactly the large, illiquid trades where getting the cost right matters most. A volume-based model, built from spread and the square-root impact law, is more work, but it is the only one of the three that tells the truth across the full range of trades a real strategy will place.

points: Fixed slippage (a flat rupee amount) and percentage-based slippage (a flat percentage) are both blind to liquidity, and both can be off by one to three orders of magnitude on large orders in illiquid names.

Volume-based slippage combines the spread-tier model from Lesson 1 with the square-root market impact model from Lesson 2, and is the only approach of the three that correctly separates a small liquid trade from a large illiquid one.

Simpler models tend to validate well on easy cases, small orders in liquid names, which is precisely what makes them dangerous: they pass every check you happen to run before failing on the trades that matter.
Percentage-based slippage is a defensible shortcut only for strategies confined to liquid, large-cap names at modest participation rates; anything beyond that requires a volume-based model.
